title: Kapila Teaches His Mother
word: each as a lens for a week
hook: Devahuti, worn out by wanting, asks her son Kapila how to be free: the second pair of lenses, Samkhya and Yoga

screen: `A RELIABLE WORD, NOT A RUMOR.` · `THE SECOND PAIR.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata's third book, Devahuti has lived a long, full life. Her husband, the sage Kardama, has gone off to the forest. Her son stays with her. His name is Kapila, and tradition remembers a sage named Kapila as the founder of Samkhya. One day she comes to him and says, in effect: I'm worn out by the cravings of my senses. I've been lost in a darkness that won't lift. You've come to be my light. Teach me how to be free. A son becomes his mother's teacher, and what he teaches is the second pair: Samkhya and Yoga.
screen: `A MOTHER, WORN OUT BY WANTING.` → `HER SON, KAPILA.` → `TEACH ME HOW TO BE FREE.`

segments.voice: Kapila starts with the Samkhya question: who is watching? He draws the great division. On one side, prakriti, nature: everything that moves and changes, the body, the senses, even the mind and the sense of I. On the other, purusha, the self, who sees and doesn't act. The trouble, he tells her, is that the self takes nature's movements as its own. Nature does the doing, and the self thinks: I am doing this, I am suffering this. Then comes a line the Bhagavata is known for: the mind is the cause of bondage, and the mind is the cause of freedom. Tied to the world's pulls, it binds. Turned toward the Lord, it frees. The Bhagavata's Kapila is a devotee as well as a philosopher; the classic Samkhya texts don't speak of God this way. Now the Yoga lens. Its question: what is the mind doing right now? Patanjali's Yoga Sutra defines yoga as the stilling of the mind's movements. Then the seer rests in its own nature; otherwise it seems to take the mind's shapes. How do the movements settle? By practice and by letting go. That's the teaching under these two: in Hindu thought, you are not your passing states. Anger, fear, a speech building in your head: all of it is nature moving. The one who sees it isn't burning. Devahuti, the Bhagavata says, practiced what her son taught her, and reached freedom.
screen: `SAMKHYA: WHO IS WATCHING?` · `THE MIND BINDS, THE MIND FREES.` · `YOGA: STILLING THE MIND.` · `YOU ARE NOT YOUR PASSING STATES.`

segments.voice: Let a recent flash of anger or worry come to mind. With the Samkhya lens, notice that all of it, the heat, the story, even the I that was hurt, is being seen, and rest a few breaths as the one who sees. With the Yoga lens, come back to your breath, stay a little longer than is easy, and loosen your grip on how it should have gone. If you pray, turn that mind toward the One you pray to, as Kapila told his mother; if you don't, simply let it settle.
Each as a lens for a week. Today, the second pair: Samkhya asks who is watching, Yoga asks what the mind is doing. Today's word.

howItsDone: Samkhya and Yoga are traditionally studied as a pair, and many Hindus first meet Samkhya's ideas in the Bhagavata, where Kapila teaches his mother Devahuti; the Yoga Sutra is the guide many use for stilling the mind.

chat.meaning: Kapila taught Devahuti that the self watches nature's movements; the Yoga Sutra stills the mind by practice and letting go, so a hot moment is where the practice happens.
